Q115861632.summary: In the centre of this ivory triptych Christ rises in a mandorla carried by four angels, while beneath him the Virgin stands with raised arms among two groups of six disciples. On the wings, apostles stand beneath arches on twisted columns: on the right Peter and Andrew, recognisable by their attributes, and on the left probably Paul and Matthew. The choice of saints ties this vision of the ascended Lord to the cities of southern Italy where it was made.
facts: The Louvre suggests the saints were chosen for local reasons: Andrew is the patron of Amalfi and Matthew of Salerno.
The ivory was once inlaid with pearls.
It was given to the Louvre in 1909 by the Paris dealer Siegfried Ratzersdorfer.

cur:monumental-sant-aquilino-christ-apos.summary: In the semi-dome of a niche, a young, beardless Christ with a halo bearing the Chi-Rho sits at the centre, raising his right hand as he speaks, while the twelve apostles sit around him in a semicircle against a gold ground; a box of scrolls stands at his feet. Like a classical philosopher among his pupils, Christ is shown as the true teacher. It is among the earliest surviving gold-ground mosaics of Christ.
facts: The octagonal chapel, which may originally have been built as an imperial mausoleum, adjoins the late-4th-century basilica of San Lorenzo.
Wikipedia notes that the scene has been read both as a 'Traditio Legis' (Christ the Lawgiver) and as Christ the Teacher among his apostles.

wga:zearly/1/4mosaics/3various/7byzanti.summary: In the golden semi-dome of the apse the Virgin, in a dark maphorion, sits on a jewelled throne with the Christ Child on her lap; he wears gold, has a cross-inscribed halo and raises his hand in blessing, while the hand of God above holds a wreath over them. Two archangels flank the throne, and beyond them stand saints and local clergy, among them Bishop Euphrasius holding a model of his church. A border of medallions of female martyrs centred on the Lamb of God frames the scene, which places the Mother of God and her Son in the position of heavenly majesty.
facts: Wikipedia describes this as the only surviving depiction of the Mother of God in the apse of an early Christian basilica in the West.
Among the figures is St Maurus, first bishop of Poreč, and a small child identified by inscription as Euphrasius, son of the archdeacon Claudius.
The Euphrasian Basilica has been on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 1997.
wga:zearly/1/4mosaics/3various/7byzanti.notes: WGA dates the mosaic c. 540, but the present basilica was built from 553 under Bishop Euphrasius (construction took about ten years), so the apse mosaic is redated to the mid-6th century. Location spelling corrected from 'Poreè'.
